title: The Selma to Montgomery Marches
traveller: Marchers of the Selma voting rights campaign
intro: Three marches were held in 1965 along the 54 mile (87 km) highway from Selma, Alabama, to the state capital, Montgomery. Nonviolent activists organised them to demand that African American citizens be allowed to exercise their constitutional right to vote.
ending: On 25 March 25,000 people stood at the steps of the Alabama State Capitol. That night Viola Liuzzo, a white mother of five from Detroit, was shot dead by Ku Klux Klan members while ferrying marchers back to Selma. President Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965.

legs.title: Selma, Marion and the road to the bridge

stops.text: Martin Luther King Jr. addressed a mass meeting here in defiance of an injunction against such gatherings, and the Selma Voting Rights Campaign officially began.
stops.quote: The Selma Voting Rights Campaign officially started on January 2, 1965, when King addressed a mass meeting in Brown Chapel A.M.E. Church in defiance of the anti-meeting injunction.

stops.text: C. T. Vivian led a march to the Perry County courthouse in Marion. Troopers attacked the marchers after the street lights were turned off, and trooper James Bonard Fowler shot Jimmie Lee Jackson in a café. Jackson died eight days later.
stops.quote: On February 18, 1965, C. T. Vivian led a march to the courthouse in Marion, the county seat of neighboring Perry County, to protest the arrest of James Orange.

stops.text: At a meeting after Jackson's death, with emotions running high, James Bevel called for a march from Selma to Montgomery to speak to Governor George Wallace about the killing, hoping to turn anger towards a nonviolent goal.
stops.quote: During a public meeting at Zion United Methodist Church in Marion on February 28 after Jackson's death, emotions were running high.

stops.text: An estimated 525 to 600 marchers crossed the bridge and met state troopers and county possemen. The troopers shoved and beat them with nightsticks, fired tear gas and charged on horseback. Seventeen marchers were hospitalised. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.
stops.quote: The protest went according to plan until the marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge, where they encountered a wall of state troopers and county posse waiting for them on the other side.

legs.title: The turned-back march and the third march

stops.text: King led about 2,500 marchers onto the bridge, held a short prayer and turned them around, obeying a court order and an agreement made with Sheriff Clark and Al Lingo. Many marchers were confused.
stops.quote: King led about 2,500 marchers out on the Edmund Pettus Bridge and held a short prayer session before turning them around, thereby obeying the court order preventing them from making the full march, and following the agreement made by Collins, Lingo, and Clark.

stops.text: That evening in Selma four Ku Klux Klan members clubbed three white Unitarian Universalist ministers. Activists took the worst injured, James Reeb of Boston, to Birmingham, where he died with his wife beside him.
stops.quote: Reeb died on Thursday, March 11 at University Hospital, with his wife by his side.

stops.text: Close to 8,000 people assembled here to begin the walk to Montgomery. The Alabama National Guard, under federal control, escorted the march after Judge Johnson ruled it could go ahead.
stops.quote: On Sunday, March 21, close to 8,000 people assembled at Brown Chapel A.M.E. Church to commence the trek to Montgomery.

stops.text: Several thousand marchers reached the final campsite on the outskirts of Montgomery. That night a Stars for Freedom rally was held on a makeshift stage, with Harry Belafonte, Joan Baez and Nina Simone among the performers.
stops.quote: By evening, several thousand marchers had reached the final campsite at the City of St. Jude, a complex on the outskirts of Montgomery.

stops.text: 25,000 people marched from St. Jude to the Capitol steps, where King gave the speech "How Long, Not Long". State troopers blocked the door, and a secretary of Governor Wallace took the petition.
stops.quote: On Thursday, March 25, 25,000 people marched from St. Jude to the steps of the State Capitol Building where King delivered the speech "How Long, Not Long".

notes: Liuzzo's killing has no named place, so it is in the ending only (article: assassinated later that night while ferrying marchers back to Selma; FBI informant Gary Rowe was in the car). Lowndes County campsites (22-23 March) are not named as places, so left out; Hayneville is named only in passing. Birmingham stop: article says 'University Hospital'; wp title UAB Hospital is my best match, check. Marion is used twice (two events); Brown Chapel and the bridge each appear twice. Good Samaritan Hospital (Jackson's death) left out: no own article confirmed. Jackson's death date 26 February is in the article intro, not the Marion paragraph.
